title: Dead Band — Chapter 1: Is Anyone Out There?
intro:
Get a notebook and pencil. They are your most important weapons. Write down frequencies, callsigns, procedures, formulas, and anything else that might keep you alive. Use your ham radio study materials whenever you need them. Looking things up is not cheating. Out here, knowing where to find an answer is part of knowing the answer.

The radio in front of you is already powered on. Someone left it tuned to 146.520 MHz, FM, at low power.

A handwritten note taped beside the transmit button reads:

LISTEN FIRST.
KNOW YOUR FREQUENCY.
USE ONLY THE POWER YOU NEED.
THEY ARE LISTENING TOO.

hello.text: K7MVR listening on five-two. Any surviving station receiving, listen before you transmit. Again: K7MVR listening on 146.520.

responses.feedback: You listen. No other station answers.

too-fast.text: Easy. Listen first. You don't know who else might be using the frequency. And these days, you really don't know who might be listening.

listened.text: The frequency remains quiet except for K7MVR. The display reads 146.520 MHz. Mode: FM.

responses.feedback: You call the station using its callsign followed by your own.

responses.text: CQ CQ CQ! Anybody out there?
responses.feedback: You already know the station you want. Call K7MVR directly.

contact.text: K7DBN, K7MVR. Well, that's a pleasant surprise. I'm Mara. And whoever left you that radio knew what they were doing. You're on 146.520 MHz FM — the national 2-meter simplex calling frequency. Simplex means we're transmitting and receiving directly on the same frequency. This frequency is useful for making contact, but we shouldn't occupy it longer than necessary. Write this down: 146.550 MHz, FM. Move there and call me again.

arrival.text: K7DBN, K7MVR. Good. Now we're off the calling frequency. Look at your radio. Frequency tells you where you're transmitting. Mode tells the radio how to put information onto the signal. Power helps determine how far that signal may be heard. The Watchers have direction-finding equipment. Every transmission tells them a radio is out here somewhere. So what power should you use?

responses.text: The lowest power that gives reliable communication.
responses.feedback: Correct. Use the minimum power necessary for reliable communication.

responses.text: Maximum power, so the transmission is over faster.
responses.feedback: More power can make you detectable from farther away. Start with only what you need.

power-correct.text: Exactly. Low power isn't always enough. Sometimes we'll need more. But don't use power you don't need. Around here, every unnecessary watt is another chance for someone to hear you.

elias.text: Let's see if you can make another contact. Elias is nearby. Callsign K7ELN. He's monitoring 146.580 MHz FM simplex. Start low. If he can't copy you, increase power one step.

hello.text: K7DBN, K7ELN. I have you, but you're weak. Don't jump straight to maximum power. Bring it up one step and try again.

responses.feedback: Increase power only as much as necessary.

power-up.text: Much better. That's enough. The right amount of power isn't 'as much as the radio can make.' It's enough to establish reliable communication.

repeater-clue.text: Mara wants you on RIDGE-1 next. That's a repeater. Unlike simplex, you transmit on one frequency and receive on another. Write this down: repeater output 146.940 MHz. Standard 2-meter offset: 600 kHz. This repeater uses a minus offset. Set the radio for 146.940 MHz FM with a -0.600 MHz shift. Then try calling Mara.

failure.text: You transmit. Nothing comes back. No repeater response. No Mara.

elias-help.text: K7DBN, K7ELN. I heard you on the repeater input. Your frequency and offset are right, but RIDGE-1 isn't opening for you. You're missing the access tone. Set CTCSS transmit to 100.0 Hz. It's a subaudible tone the repeater listens for before it opens. It isn't encryption and it doesn't make the conversation private.

success.text: K7DBN, K7MVR through RIDGE-1. There you are. You're listening to the repeater on 146.940, but with a minus 600 kilohertz offset your radio transmits to it on 146.340. The repeater receives you there and retransmits you on 146.940 from a much better location.

responses.text: So the repeater lets us communicate beyond direct simplex range.
responses.feedback: Right. Its location and antenna can greatly extend useful coverage.

responses.text: So the repeater increases the power of my radio.
responses.feedback: Not your transmitter power. The repeater receives your signal and retransmits it from its own station.

tone-question.text: And what did that 100 Hz CTCSS tone do?

responses.text: It allowed my transmission to access the repeater.
It encrypted our conversation from the Watchers.
responses.feedback: No. CTCSS is not encryption. Anyone capable of receiving the transmission can still hear it.

mission.text: Good. Tutorial's over. Now we have a real problem. Medical convoy MED-3 missed its morning check-in. They were supposed to report to the valley emergency net. Net control is K7NCS on 147.150 MHz, FM, plus 600 kilohertz, CTCSS 100.0. Don't just barge in. Find the net, listen, and follow net control's instructions.

traffic.text: K7NCS to all stations: stand by. Emergency traffic in progress. K7ELN, continue your report.

responses.text: K7NCS, K7DBN! I'm looking for MED-3!
responses.feedback: Net control told all other stations to stand by.
You wait while the emergency traffic is completed.

interrupted.text: K7DBN, stand by. Emergency traffic has priority. I'll call you when I'm ready.

called.text: K7DBN, K7NCS. Go ahead with your traffic.

responses.text: K7NCS, K7DBN. I'm trying to locate medical convoy MED-3. They missed their scheduled check-in.
Has anybody seen the medical convoy?
responses.feedback: On a directed net, communicate through net control unless instructed otherwise.

report.text: K7DBN, copy. Last traffic from MED-3 was relayed by K7RPT. He reported interference near the east pass and said the convoy might switch to simplex if they lost the repeater. His last known monitoring frequency was 146.550 MHz FM. Try there. Keep your transmission brief.

weak.text: ...DBN... MED-3... receiving you weak but readable... repeater unusable from this side of the pass...

responses.text: MED-3, K7DBN. I copy you. Give me your status.

responses.feedback: The signal is readable. More power may not be necessary.

status.text: K7DBN, MED-3. Convoy intact. Bridge on Route Four is blocked. We diverted east and lost repeater coverage. We need net control to tell the relief team not to follow us onto Route Four. Repeat: Route Four blocked. Relief team must divert east.

responses.text: Copy: Route Four blocked. Relief team divert east. I'll relay.
K7NCS, K7DBN with traffic from MED-3. Route Four is blocked. MED-3 diverted east. Relief team must not use Route Four.

responses.feedback: Net control needs the actual message, not just a summary that they're safe.

need-message.text: K7DBN, I need their traffic. What does MED-3 need us to know?

responses.text: Route Four is blocked. MED-3 diverted east. Relief team must not use Route Four.

resolution.text: K7DBN, K7NCS. Relief team copied the message. They're turning east now. Good work. Clear when ready.
